L206: On arriving at Savannah, the hunters found that the fugitives had sold the horses and trap, and embarked as free white persons, for New York. Slator's disappointment and rascality so preyed upon his base mind, that he, like Judas, went and hanged himself.
L207: 
L208: As soon as Frank and Mary were safe, they endeavoured to redeem their good mother. But, alas! she was gone; she had passed on to the realm of spirit life.
L209: In due time Frank learned from his friends in Georgia where his little brother and sister dwelt. So he wrote at once to purchase them, but the persons with whom they lived would not sell them.
L210: After failing in several attempts to buy them, Frank cultivated large whiskers and moustachios, cut off his hair, put on a wig and glasses, and went down as a white man, and stopped in the neighbourhood where his sister was; and after see- ing her and also his little brother, arrangements were made for them to meet at a particular place on a Sunday, which they did, and got safely off.
L211: I saw Frank myself, when he came for the little twins. Though I was then quite a lad, I well remember being highly delighted by hearing him tell how nicely he and Mary had served Slator.
L212: 
L213: Frank had so completely disguised or changed his appearance that his little sister did not know him, and would not speak till he showed their mother's likeness; the sight of which melted her to tears,—for she knew the face. Frank might have said to her
L214: "'O, Emma! O, my sister, speak to me!
L215:  Dost thou not know me, that I am thy brother?
L216:  Come to me, little Emma, thou shalt dwell
L217:  With me henceforth, and know no care or want.'
L218:  Emma was silent for a space, as if
L219:  'Twere hard to summon up a human voice."
L220: Frank and Mary's mother was my wife's own
L221: dear aunt.
L222: 
L223: After this great diversion from our narrative, which I hope dear reader, you will excuse, I shall return at once to it.
L224: My wife was torn from her mother's embrace in childhood, and taken to a distant part of the country.
L225: She had seen so many other children separated from their parents in this cruel man- ner, that the mere thought of her ever becoming the mother of a child, to linger out a miserable existence under the wretched system of American slavery, appeared to fill her very soul with horror; and as she had taken what I felt to be an important view of her condition, I did not, at first, press the marriage, but agreed to assist her in trying to devise some plan by which we might escape from our unhappy condition, and then be married.
L226: We thought of plan after plan, but they all seemed crowded with insurmountable difficulties. We knew it was unlawful for any public convey- ance to take us as passengers, without our master's consent.
L227: We were also perfectly aware of the startling fact, that had we left without this consent the professional slave-hunters would have soon had their ferocious bloodhounds baying on our track, and in a short time we should have been dragged back to slavery, not to fill the more favour- able situations which we had just left, but to be separated for life, and put to the very meanest and most laborious drudgery; or else have been tortured to death as examples, in order to strike terror into the hearts of others, and thereby pre- vent them from even attempting to escape from their cruel taskmasters.
L228: It is a fact worthy of remark, that nothing seems to give the slaveholders so much pleasure as the catching and torturing of fugitives. They had much rather take the keen and poisonous lash, and with it cut their poor trembling victims to atoms, than allow one of them to escape to a free country, and expose the infamous system from which he fled.
L229: The greatest excitement prevails at a slave-hunt. The slaveholders and their hired ruffians appear to take more pleasure in this inhuman pursuit than English sportsmen do in chasing a fox or a stag. Therefore, knowing what we should have been compelled to suffer, if caught and taken back, we were more than anxious to hit upon a plan that would lead us safely to a land of liberty.
L230: But, after puzzling our brains for years, we were reluctantly driven to the sad conclusion, that it was almost impossible to escape from slavery in Georgia, and travel 1,000 miles across the slave States.
L231: We therefore resolved to get the consent of our owners, be married, settle down in slavery, and endeavour to make ourselves as comfortable as possible under that system; but at the same time ever to keep our dim eyes steadily fixed upon the glimmering hope of liberty, and earnestly pray God mercifully to assist us to escape from our unjust thraldom.
L232: We were married, and prayed and toiled on till December, 1848, at which time (as I have stated) a plan suggested itself that proved quite success- ful, and in eight days after it was first thought of we were free from the horrible trammels of slavery, and glorifying God who had brought us safely out of a land of bondage.
L233: Knowing that slaveholders have the privilege of taking their slaves to any part of the country they think proper, it occurred to me that, as my wife was nearly white, I might get her to disguise herself as an invalid gentleman, and assume to be my master, while I could attend as his slave, and that in this manner we might effect our escape. After I thought of the plan, I sug- gested it to my wife, but at first she shrank from the idea.
L234: She thought it was almost impossible for her to assume that disguise, and travel a dis- tance of 1,000 miles across the slave States. How- ever, on the other hand, she also thought of her condition. She saw that the laws under which we lived did not recognize her to be a woman, but a mere chattel, to be bought and sold, or otherwise dealt with as her owner might see fit. Therefore the more she contemplated her helpless condition, the more anxious she was to escape from it.
L235: So she said, "I think it is almost too much for us to undertake; however, I feel that God is on our side, and with his assistance, notwithstanding all the difficulties, we shall be able to succeed. There- fore, if you will purchase the disguise, I will try to carry out the plan."
L236: But after I concluded to purchase the disguise, I was afraid to go to any one to ask him to sell me the articles. It is unlawful in Georgia for a white man to trade with slaves without the master's con- sent. But, notwithstanding this, many persons will sell a slave any article that he can get the money to buy. Not that they sympathize with the slave, but merely because his testimony is not admitted in court against a free white person.
L237: Therefore, with little difficulty I went to dif- ferent parts of the town, at odd times, and purchased things piece by piece, (except the trowsers which she found necessary to make,) and took them home to the house where my wife resided.
L238: She being a ladies' maid, and a favourite slave in the family, was allowed a little room to herself; and amongst other pieces of furniture which I had made in my overtime, was a chest of drawers; so when I took the articles home, she locked them up carefully in these drawers. No one about the premises knew that she had anything of the kind. So when we fancied we had everything ready the time was fixed for the flight.
L239: But we knew it would not do to start off without first getting our master's con- sent to be away for a few days. Had we left with- out this, they would soon have had us back into slavery, and probably we should never have got another fair opportunity of even attempting to escape.
L240: Some of the best slaveholders will sometimes give their favourite slaves a few days' holiday at Christmas time; so, after no little amount of per- severance on my wife's part, she obtained a pass from her mistress, allowing her to be away for a few days. The cabinet-maker with whom I worked gave me a similar paper, but said that he needed my services very much, and wished me to return as soon as the time granted was up.
L241: I thanked him kindly; but somehow I have not been able to make it convenient to return yet; and, as the free air of good old England agrees so well with my wife and our dear little ones, as well as with myself, it is not at all likely we shall return at present to the "peculiar in- stitution" of chains and stripes.
L242: On reaching my wife's cottage she handed me her pass, and I showed mine, but at that time neither of us were able to read them. It is not only unlawful for slaves to be taught to read, but in some of the States there are heavy penalties at- tached, such as fines and imprisonment, which will be vigorously enforced upon any one who is humane enough to violate the so-called law.
L243: 
L244: The following case will serve to show how per- sons are treated in the most enlightened slavehold- ing community.
L245: ##### "INDICTMENT.
L246: 
L247: COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA, } In the Circuit
L248: NORFOLK COUNTY, ss.} Court.
L249: The Grand Jurors empannelled in the body of the said County on their oath present, that Margaret Doug- lass, being an evil disposed person, not having the fear of God before her eyes, but moved and insti- gated by the devil, wickedly, maliciously, and feloniously, on the fourth day of July, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and fifty- four, at Norfolk, in said County, did teach a certain black girl named Kate to read in the Bible, to the great displeasure of Almighty God, to the per- nicious example of others in like case offending, contrary to the form of the statute in such case made and provided, and against the peace and dignity of the Commonwealth of Virginia.
L250: "VICTOR VAGABOND, Prosecuting Attorney."
L251: "On this indictment Mrs. Douglass was arraigned as a necessary matter of form, tried, found guilty of course; and Judge Scalaway, before whom she was tried, having consulted with Dr. Adams, or- dered the sheriff to place Mrs. Douglass in the prisoner's box, when he addressed her as follows: 'Margaret Douglass, stand up. You are guilty of one of the vilest crimes that ever disgraced society; and the jury have found you so. You have taught a slave girl to read in the Bible.
L252: No enlightened society can exist where such offences go unpun- ished. The Court, in your case, do not feel for you one solitary ray of sympathy, and they will inflict on you the utmost penalty of the law. In any other civilized country you would have paid the forfeit of your crime with your life, and the Court have only to regret that such is not the law in this country. The sentence for your offence is, that you be imprisoned one month in the county jail, and that you pay the costs of this prosecution.
L253: Sheriff, remove the prisoner to jail.' On the pub- lication of these proceedings, the Doctors of Divinity preached each a sermon on the necessity of obeying the laws; the New York Observer noticed with much pious gladness a revival of religion on Dr. Smith's plantation in Georgia, among his slaves; while the Journal of Commerce commended this political preaching of the Doctors of Divinity because it favoured slavery. Let us do nothing to offend our Southern brethren."
L254: However, at first, we were highly delighted at the idea of having gained permission to be absent for a few days; but when the thought flashed across my wife's mind, that it was customary for travellers to register their names in the visitors' book at hotels, as well as in the clearance or Custom-house book at Charleston, South Carolina —it made our spirits droop within us.
L255: So, while sitting in our little room upon the verge of despair, all at once my wife raised her head, and with a smile upon her face, which was a moment before bathed in tears, said, "I think I have it!" I asked what it was. She said, "I think I can make a poultice and bind up my right hand in a sling, and with propriety ask the officers to register my name for me." I thought that would do.
L256: It then occurred to her that the smoothness of her face might betray her; so she decided to make another poultice, and put it in a white handkerchief to be worn under the chin, up the cheeks, and to tie over the head. This nearly hid the expression of the countenance, as well as the beardless chin.
L257: 
L258: The poultice is left off in the engraving, because the likeness could not have been taken well with it on.
L259: My wife, knowing that she would be thrown a good deal into the company of gentlemen, fancied that she could get on better if she had something to go over the eyes; so I went to a shop and bought a pair of green spectacles. This was in the evening.
L260: We sat up all night discussing the plan, and making preparations. Just before the time arrived, in the morning, for us to leave, I cut off my wife's hair square at the back of the head, and got her to dress in the disguise and stand out on the floor. I found that she made a most respectable looking gentleman.
L261: My wife had no ambition whatever to assume this disguise, and would not have done so had it been possible to have obtained our liberty by more simple means; but we knew it was not customary in the South for ladies to travel with male servants; and therefore, notwithstanding my wife's fair com- plexion, it would have been a very difficult task for her to have come off as a free white lady, with me as her slave; in fact, her not being able to write would have made this quite impossible.
L262: We knew that no public conveyance would take us, or any other slave, as a passenger, without our master's consent. This consent could never be obtained to pass into a free State. My wife's being muffled in the poultices, &c., furnished a plausible excuse for avoiding general conversation, of which most Yankee travellers are passionately fond.

L134@P3: name Hougoumont was offensive
L135@P3: to them. In 1856 when the Crimean War ceased Hougoumont reverted to its original name, and
L136@P3: was placed back on the England–
L137@P3: India run. It was, however, not
L138@P3: entirely restricted to that route, as
L139@P3: in 1866 it carried 335 assisted emigrants to Melbourne.
L140@P3: In 1867 Hougoumont, by this time
L141@P3: owned by someone named Luscombe from London, was chartered to take 280 convicts to
L142@P3: Western Australia. The ship departed Portsmouth on 12 October
L143@P3: 1867. Besides the convicts there
L144@P3: were 44 pensioner guards, 18 wives of the guards,
L145@P3: 25 of their children, four prison warders and their
L146@P3: families and five passengers on board. The master of the Hougoumont was Captain William
L147@P3: Cousins or Cozens, and the surgeon superintendent is variously given as William Smith or
L148@P3: Brownlow.
L149@P3: Among the convicts on the Hougoumont were 62
L150@P3: Irish political prisoners from the Irish Republican
L151@P3: Brotherhood, better known as Fenians. These
L152@P3: were people who had been found guilty of taking
L153@P3: part in the 1867 Fenian Rising. Among them
L154@P3: were 17 classed as military Fenians. These were
L155@P3: men who had been serving with the British Army,
L156@P3: and had been therefore found guilt by courts martial of treason, mutinous conduct or desertion. It
L157@P3: has been reported that the transport of political
L158@P3: prisoners contravened the agreement between
L159@P3: Britain and Western Australia. Also the transport
L160@P3: of military Fenians was most unusual as the British Government had a firm policy against the
L161@P3: transport of military prisoners. Among the 17
L162@P3: military Fenians were seven who later came to
L163@P3: prominence by escaping from Western Australia.
L164@P3: They were John Boyle O’Reilly, James Wilson,
L165@P3: Michael Harrington, Robert Cranston, Thomas
L166@P3: Darragh, Thomas Hassett and Martin Hogan.
L167@P3: These latter six had been sentenced to life imprisonment, O’Reilly’s sentence was 20 years.
L168@P3: The Hougoumont arrived in Fremantle on 9 January 1868. One convict, No.9689 Thomas
L169@P3: Cochrane, had died during the voyage. This was
L170@P3: the last shipment of convicts to Australia. The
L171@P3: Hougoumont ended its life in 1885 as a store hulk
L172@P3: during the building of the Firth of Forth Bridge.
L173@P3: As for seven of the military Fenian prisoners, their
L174@P3: story made Western Australian history. In 1869
L175@P3: O’Reilly escaped and made his way to America,
L176@P3: settling in Boston where he became editor of The
L177@P3: Pilot newspaper. Although a number of the Fenians had been issued pardons, the military Fenians
L178@P3: remained as prisoners. One of them, James Wilson, wrote a letter to John Devoy, a reporter for
L179@P3: the New York Herald, asking for help to escape.
L180@P3: Devoy discussed the matter with O’Reilly and

L186@P4: Davits and whale boat gear were rigged, a forecastle built for the crew and other modifications

L191@P4: The vessel cost $5,500 to purchase, and a further

L193@P4: Anthony the Catalpa sailed from New Bedford

L195@P4: were purposely made up largely of Kanakas, Malays, and Africans, since they were likely to be
L196@P4: less suspicious than other sailors… (Pease, 1897:
L197@P4: 78). The crew were not informed of the Catalpa’s destination or the proposed attempt to rescue
L198@P4: the Fenians, but thought they were on a whaling
L199@P4: voyage to New Zealand. The barque arrived at
L200@P4: Bunbury on 28 March 1876, having gone whaling

L203@P4: the Catalpa, the fourth gaoled for a week. At the
L204@P4: end of his sentence Captain Anthony refused to
L205@P4: let the deserter back on board.
L206@P4: Two Fenians, John Breslin and Tom Desmond,
L207@P4: had meanwhile travelled to Fremantle to arrange
L208@P4: the escape of the convicts from Fremantle Gaol.
L209@P4: On 17 April 1876 Wilson, Harrington, Cranston,
L210@P4: Darragh, Hassett and Hogan, who were with a
L211@P4: working party outside the prison, absconded, and
L212@P4: were taken to Rockingham by Breslin and Desmond. They were then taken by whale-boat out
L213@P4: to the Catalpa which was waiting about nine
L214@P4: miles offshore, well outside the 3-mile limit.

L257@P6: hen I saw John Parry again with the
L258@P6: Dhipirri survey results, he asked me how
L259@P6: I felt about delivering a 60-foot windmill, water tank and associated piping and gear for
L260@P6: a bore installation at a place called Raymangirr, in
L261@P6: Arnhem Bay. The windmill would be in kit form,
L262@P6: with six-metre maximum pipe lengths, and the
L263@P6: Southern Cross water tank panels would be in a
L264@P6: crate. I was delighted with the prospect, and even
L265@P6: more so when he suggested that I could go to Darwin to pick up the load and cart it back. In terms
L266@P6: of economics, the Department was faced with regular barge freight from Darwin to Gove, then the
L267@P6: logistics of getting the gear from Gove to Raymangirr. The barge operators charged $3,000 at
L268@P6: that time for a diversion to a non-standard destination, on top of the usual cartage rate. In addition,
L269@P6: John asked me to add into my price a three-week
L270@P6: contract period to assist with the windmill erection post-delivery. I spent a couple of days mulling over the proposition, and tendered a price that
L271@P6: was accepted forthwith.
L272@P6: We set off for Darwin on March 24, taking along
L273@P6: Cabbage and Shan’s seven-year old son, Josh, for
L274@P6: the ride. We dropped off a roll of two-inch poly
L275@P6: pipe and unloaded a forty-four of petrol at MataMata on the way, then went on to Elcho to deliver
L276@P6: four more rolls of poly pipe and fittings to an outstation in the Howard Channel, called Mapuru.
L277@P6: New navigation markers leading over the shallows
L278@P6: into Cadell Strait were a welcome surprise. The
L279@P6: old outer pole had been replaced with port and
L280@P6: starboard markers, and another new outer pole
L281@P6: placed a little further out. The new poles, complete with top-markers, made it easier to follow
L282@P6: the channel, but they were still difficult to find on
L283@P6: high spring tides when there was not much showing above water. Another new marker had also
L284@P6: been placed further down the channel to indicate
L285@P6: the narrow passage where the course required a
L286@P6: switch from one side of the strait to the other between two consecutive sandbars.
L287@P6: Mapuru Landing was about ten miles from the
L288@P6: barge landing at Wapuruwa, and the channel was
L289@P6: formally uncharted as far as depths and hazards
L290@P6: were concerned. We hired a local dinghy, transhipped the poly pipe, and I set off with a local
L291@P6: bloke from the outstation, called Bakbirr, who
L292@P6: was to guide me to the landing. We travelled over
L293@P6: the low tide so I could draw up a mud map of the
L294@P6: twists and turns and obstacles, and anchored for a
L295@P6: while at the bottom of the tide, near a shallow reef
L296@P6: obstructing the channel, to get accurate soundings
L297@P6: with a lead line.
L298@P6: Bakbirr was an intelligent and serious young man
L299@P6: in his late twenties who understood English
L300@P6: enough to make some communication possible. I
L301@P6: noticed that his conversation was frequently interjected with the word “nowie”, and after a time I
L302@P6: asked, “Bakbirr, what does “nowie” mean?” He
L303@P6: looked thoughtful as he murmured to himself,
L304@P6: “Nowie… nowie… what dat “nowie” mean?”
L305@P6: After a reflective pause, he gathered his thoughts,
L306@P6: and explained, “When you want to know someting
L307@P6: (pause), and you don’t know what dat someting is
L308@P6: (pause), den (with an air of triumph:) dat “nowie”
L309@P6: tell you what dat someting is!” I took it that he
L310@P6: was referring to some benign spirit that was called
L311@P6: upon to supply answers to the unknown, and I was
L312@P6: bemused later to discover that “nowie” is in fact a
L313@P6: simple filler word, much the same us “um” or
L314@P6: “ah” in English. With elegant simplicity, Bakbirr’s explanation was perfect.
L315@P6: A couple of days later, we headed off from Elcho
L316@P6: to Darwin. A light south-easterly wind had been
L317@P6: tending for a few days, heralding the beginning of
L318@P6: the Dry Season, and we had a smooth and uneventful trip, mainly day sailing and anchoring in
L319@P6: shelter along the way overnight.
L320@P6: We were in Darwin for three weeks while Singa
L321@P6: Betina was careened and anti-fouled, supplies and
L322@P6: spares restocked, and the windmill and water tank
L323@P6: loaded on board by crane from a local jetty. Bundles of angle-iron framing, piping and equipment
L324@P6: were manhandled down below, with some longer
L325@P6: pieces and odd bits that would not fit in the jigsaw
L326@P6: puzzle of available space being secured on deck.
L327@P6: The water tank panels came packed in a low crate,
L328@P6: which sat tightly between the engine room hatch
L329@P6: and the compass binnacle on the back deck. Fuel
L330@P6: was cheaper in Darwin than Gove, so we filled up
L331@P6: our forty-fours, and spent another day or two lashing everything down and rationalising the weight
L332@P6: distribution. A couple of bulky rolls of two-inch
L333@P6: poly pipe added to the clutter on deck, and getting
L334@P6: around the obstacles became a nimble exercise.
L335@P6: The 30th April 1983 saw us on our way for the delivery to Raymangirr. As we cleared the harbour
L336@P6: and set course for the Vernon Islands, I was perturbed to find the compass behaving erratically.
L337@P6: My Time on Singa Betina
L338@P6-7: The tenth episode of Ted Whiteaker’s tale. 8
L339@P7: The presence of the metal mass of the water tank
L340@P7: in the crate so close to the compass was affecting
L341@P7: the magnetic field and throwing the readings out
L342@P7: wildly. We resorted to the use of our spare handbearing compass, and plugged on.
L343@P7: After passing through the Vernons, there was a
L344@P7: considerable swell rolling down from the north;
L345@P7: the remnants of the northwest monsoon and recent low-pressure systems of the past Wet Season. Late in the afternoon, young Josh was
L346@P7: perched on the taffrail attempting to relieve himself over the stern when we pitched into another
L347@P7: oncoming swell, and in the corner of my eye I
L348@P7: noticed a windmill-flurry of arms and legs as he
L349@P7: lost his balance and fell overboard. We were motor sailing, and with the sails up it would take a
L350@P7: few minutes to drop the rig and turn around to
L351@P7: pick him up. I yelled out, “HANG ON – WE’LL

L360@P7: We passed abeam Cape Don lighthouse around
